topic: Inverse square law for flash/light: double the distance = 1/4 of the light (same light over 4x the area), 3x = 1/9; 1/4 light = 2 stops, compensate by opening the aperture two stops (f/8 to f/4)
lines: Move your flash twice as far away, and you don't get half the light.
Light spreads out as it travels. At double the distance, the same light covers four times the area.
At triple the distance, nine times the area. One ninth of the light.
Four times the distance? One sixteenth. The light dies fast.
Four times the distance? One sixteenth. The light dies fast.
A quarter of the light is two stops. To compensate, open your aperture from f eight to f four.
A quarter of the light is 2 stops. To compensate, open your aperture from f/8 to f/4.
That's why a flash close to your subject darkens the background. The background is further away, so it gets far less light.
Distance doesn't halve light. It quarters it.

youtube.title: Move Your Flash 2× Further = 1/4 of the Light (Inverse Square Law)
youtube.description:
For a point-like light source such as a flash, intensity falls with the square of the distance: double the distance and the subject receives one quarter of the light (the same light spread over four times the area); triple it and it is one ninth. A quarter of the light is two stops, so to keep the same exposure you open the aperture two stops, for example f/8 to f/4. Real softboxes and large sources deviate from the ideal law when close. The spheres shown are a simulation (1, 1/4, 1/9 light, sRGB-encoded).
#photography #flash #shorts

https://www.geofflawrence.com/inverse_square_law.html (double the flash-to-subject distance = a quarter of the illumination; need four times the light for the same exposure; that is a two-stop change, compensated by opening the aperture two f-stops)
Check: 1/2^2 = 1/4; 1/3^2 = 1/9; f/8 -> f/5.6 -> f/4 is two stops; the sphere images are a numpy simulation with I = 1/d^2.
